source: Hedge, Powell, Sumner (2018) The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
finding: Seven classic control tasks were run in two sessions. Raw RTs were reliable but conflict-cost difference scores were not. None of the behavioural measures reached ICC .8.
numbers: Studies 1 and 2 total N about 99-104; Study 3 N=40. Study 1 flanker RT cost ICC .40, while congruent RT was .74 and incongruent RT .66. Stroop RT cost ICC .60 (Study 1) and .66 (Study 2). Go/no-go commission errors .76 in both studies.
quote: None of the behavioral measures in Studies 1 and 2 exceeded reliabilities of .8
limits: Student samples; two sessions only. The flanker RT cost is the same kind of score as the ANT executive network.
agent_relevance: Do not treat one ANT-style conflict score as a stable trait. Any per-run attention probe for the agent needs many trials and averaging.

source: Hedge, Powell, Sumner (2018) The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
finding: Low error is not enough for reliability. The flanker cost had a small SEM yet low ICC, because people differ little from each other on it. Different control tasks also agree poorly with each other.
numbers: Flanker RT cost SEM 15 ms with ICC .4. Between tasks: flanker RT cost vs Stroop RT cost observed r=.14 and disattenuated rho=.25 (N=100).
quote: measurement error alone does not predict reliability
limits: Disattenuated correlations rest on uncertain reliabilities (wide CIs).
agent_relevance: Weak agreement between tasks means 'executive control' from one task may not generalise. Do not assume one conflict test captures one control capacity.

source: Hedge, Powell, Sumner (2018) The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
finding: The authors argue the paradox is structural: experimental tasks are built to shrink between-person variance, and reliability is between-person variance divided by total variance.
numbers: Study 3 (N=40) used Navon and SNARC tasks and showed the same pattern of group effects with poor reliability.
limits: Applies to every subtraction score, including ANT alerting (no cue minus double cue) and orienting.
agent_relevance: Expect the ANT alerting and orienting subtractions to be weakly stable.

source: Kucina et al. (2023) Calibration of cognitive tests to address the reliability paradox for decision-conflict tasks
finding: Five experiments tried to fix the paradox. Gamified flanker and Stroop+Simon tasks that also required a second response to the distractor raised conflict effects and gave reliable person-level estimates in under 100 trials.
numbers: Benchmark: with trait precision .13, about 420 trials are needed for r=.8. Friedman and Miyake split-half r=.59 with 40 flanker trials (trait precision .16). Hierarchical Bayesian models, MTurk sample from 2021.
quote: produced reliable estimates of individual differences in under 100 trials per task
limits: Reliability is split-half style inside one session, so test-retest will be lower. Online sample; tasks are not the ANT.
agent_relevance: Design lesson: force processing of the distractor and use hierarchical scoring. For any conflict probe on the agent, require a response to the distractor too.

source: Ishigami and Klein (2011) Repeated measurement of the components of attention of older adults using the two versions of the Attention Network Test
finding: Ten sessions of two ANT versions in 10 older adults. All three network scores stayed significantly above zero after nine earlier sessions, so the effects are robust. One-session reliability is poor and rises when sessions are added.
numbers: N=10 older adults, 10 sessions, two ANT versions per session. Practice effects in executive and alerting scores. For RT, reliabilities were significant only when more than nine sessions were included. For error rate, alerting reliability never reached significance. With one session, ANT-I scores were generally more reliable than ANT scores.
quote: relatively poor reliability of network scores with one session of data rises to respectable levels as more data is added
limits: Very small sample, older adults only.
agent_relevance: Aggregate many trials before reading a network score. The ANT-I design is the better template for a probe.

source: Ishigami and Klein (2011) Repeated measurement of the components of attention of older adults using the two versions of the Attention Network Test
finding: Some lack of independence among the networks was found even though scores were built by orthogonal subtraction. ANT and ANT-I alerting scores in RT were larger in the ANT but strongly correlated.
numbers: ANT vs ANT-I alerting RT scores correlated r=0.96. For error rates the three network scores did not differ between versions, but the cross-version correlations for alerting and orienting were not significant.
limits: N=10, so correlations are unstable.
agent_relevance: Version choice changes what a network score means; cross-version comparisons are risky.

source: McConnell and Shore (2011) Mixing measures: testing an assumption of the attention network test
finding: Large student sample: the ANT habit of averaging over cue and flanker conditions is shaky. Component conditions of a network score correlate weakly with each other, and Cue x Flanker interactions appear inside all three networks.
numbers: N=588 undergraduates in three experiments (10 excluded). Between-network r: alerting-orienting .07, alerting-executive .01, orienting-executive -.04. Alerting, trimmed RT: neutral vs incongruent r=.11, neutral vs congruent r=.29; error rates r=.09.
quote: intranetwork correlations were surprisingly low, and Cue X Flanker interactions were found
limits: One lab; includes mood and music manipulation experiments. Independence at score level does not prove independent mechanisms.
agent_relevance: The ANT networks are not clean modules. Cue type changes flanker cost, so warning and control interact.

source: McConnell and Shore (2011) Mixing measures: testing an assumption of the attention network test
finding: Flanker interference depends on cue type. It is smaller with double and centre cues than with no cue and spatial cue in RT, but not in error rates.
numbers: Trimmed RT flanker effect differed by cue condition, t>4.3, p<.001. Error rates: no vs spatial cue t(576)=0.17, p=.87; double vs centre cue t(576)=0.77, p=.44. Executive scores across the four cue types differed even after Bonferroni correction, t>3.3, p<.001.
limits: N=588 students; trimmed means.
agent_relevance: A warning cue changes how much distractors hurt. Warn-then-act prompts for an agent may change conflict handling.

source: Habekost, Petersen, Vangkilde (2014) Testing attention: comparing the ANT with TVA-based assessment
finding: First direct ANT vs TVA comparison over three sessions. Only the ANT executive score matched TVA reliability. Alerting and orienting were weak.
numbers: N=68 young adults, 3 consecutive sessions, both tests each. Literature figures quoted in the paper: alerting and orienting retest .35-.60, executive .65-.80. All pairwise correlations between the eight parameters of the two tests small and nonsignificant, except r=.72 between two TVA parameters. After correcting for test length, orienting retest reliability equalled the least reliable TVA parameters.
quote: only the executive network score reached comparable levels
limits: Young adults only. Low cross-test correlations may mean different constructs or noise.
agent_relevance: If we need a stable attention measure, TVA-style selectivity parameters beat ANT alerting and orienting.

source: Habekost, Petersen, Vangkilde (2014) Testing attention: comparing the ANT with TVA-based assessment
finding: Both tests showed practice effects that improved some parameters and left others constant, so repeated testing mixes change with learning.
numbers: 3 sessions, N=68.
limits: Young adults.
agent_relevance: When re-running a probe after changing the agent, expect learning-like drift from repeated prompts or memory.

source: Wang et al. (2015) Improving the Attention Network Test: mixed design and non-orthogonal scoring (Sci Rep 5:10251)
finding: A mixed block and event-related ANT with non-orthogonal scoring gave better reliability and showed the networks interact in both directions.
numbers: N=50 recruited, 44 analysed (mean age 20.3). Split-half: alerting .684, orienting .588, executive .616, versus .14-.38 for alerting and orienting in earlier work as the authors quote. Score correlations: A-O r=-.310 (p=.040, not surviving Bonferroni), A-E r=.174, O-E r=.045. Directional pairs: A->O vs O->A r=-.411; A->E vs E->A r=-.348; O->E vs E->O r=.605.
limits: Students only, no moderators tested, split-half not retest. Authors read the pattern as resource competition.
agent_relevance: Interactions between networks are stable enough to model. Treat alerting, orienting and control as coupled.

source: Wang et al. (2014) A new method for computing attention network scores and relationships between attention networks (PLoS ONE 9:e89733)
finding: Abstract only. Dissecting cue-target conditions gave a larger alerting score and a smaller executive score than the original formula, and showed alerting-executive and orienting-executive interactions.
numbers: 36 participants.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC; full text not opened.
agent_relevance: The scoring formula changes the size of the scores. Record the formula whenever an ANT number is used.

source: Klein, Good, Christie (2024) Changes in the networks of attention across the lifespan: a graphical meta-analysis
finding: Graphical meta-analysis of 36 publications from the ANT Database (PRISMA-guided). Lifespan trajectories depend on cue type and signal modality.
numbers: 36 publications. Alerting reaches near-adult level by about age 12. With visual warnings alerting scores fall from childhood to old age; with auditory warnings childhood decline is robust but the few ageing studies show an increase with age. Orienting depends on cue informativeness; with uninformative cues scores keep decreasing past adolescence.
limits: Graphical, not effect-size weighted. Different ANT versions across studies. Few auditory ageing studies.
agent_relevance: The ANT is a family of tests. Cue type and version are the main moderators, so 'orienting' claims are version-specific.

source: Klein, Good, Christie (2024) Changes in the networks of attention across the lifespan: a graphical meta-analysis
finding: In adults (ages 19-75) executive control scores in RT rise with age (worse) while error-based scores trend the other way. Executive scores improve through childhood.
numbers: Opposite RT and error trends in the same 36 publications; moderate increase in orienting scores with age in adulthood.
quote: executive control scores, as measured in reaction time, increase (deterioration) from young adulthood into later adulthood
limits: Group-level means from published plots.
agent_relevance: Report both speed and accuracy. For LLMs the pair is accuracy and token cost.

source: Klein, Good, Christie (2024) Changes in the networks of attention across the lifespan: a graphical meta-analysis
finding: Child ANT versions with different cues give mixed readings of orienting, and a pair of observations from one developmental lab prevents a firm conclusion about late childhood to early adulthood.
numbers: Rueda ANT-C and ANT-O pair noted; other studies give clearer trends with uninformative cues.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Apparent group differences may be design artefacts. Check cue informativeness and modality first.

source: Luna et al. (2023) The ANTI-Vea-UGR platform: a free online resource to measure attentional networks
finding: ANTI-Vea measures the three networks plus executive and arousal vigilance in one task, lab or online. Overall scores are reliable; vigilance decrement slopes are much less so.
numbers: Overall scores had Spearman-Brown split-half above .75 in both lab and online settings (Luna 2021). Decrement slopes over six blocks are substantially less reliable. Online split-half rose with number of sessions, as in Ishigami and Klein.
limits: Review of the team's own earlier results; numbers cited, not new data.
agent_relevance: Online delivery does not harm reliability. A slope over time is the hardest thing to measure, relevant to any context-length decay metric.

source: Luna, Tortajada, Martin-Arevalo, Botta, Lupianez (2022) A vigilance decrement comes along with an executive control decrement: testing the resource-control theory
finding: Reanalysis of 617 people on the ANTI-Vea: executive control gets worse with time on task, along with the vigilance decrement. Support for resource-control theory, with small effects.
numbers: N=617 (314 lab, 303 online; 445 women; mean age 22.78). Interference grew linearly: RT F(4.86,2852.72)=9.69, p<.001, partial eta squared .02; errors F(4.91,2885.48)=2.50, p=.029, partial eta squared<.01; inverse efficiency F(4.84,2789.60)=8.33, partial eta squared .01. Linear trend for RT t(587)=5.86.
quote: given the small effect sizes observed in our large sample size
limits: Small effects even at N=617. An earlier ANT study (Zholdassova 2021) did not see the decline, but the ANT cannot measure vigilance.
agent_relevance: Control quality drifts over time on task, so long runs may need re-checks. Compare the long-list collapse in LLM Stroop (Patel 2025).

source: Luna, Tortajada, Martin-Arevalo, Botta, Lupianez (2022) A vigilance decrement comes along with an executive control decrement: testing the resource-control theory
finding: Executive vigilance and arousal vigilance are separable. Only the executive component of the vigilance decrement tracked the control decline.
numbers: Same N=617. The decline in hits (executive vigilance) was steeper in people whose interference grew; arousal vigilance was not modulated.
limits: Individual-differences analysis, one task.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of sustained attention: staying sharp for rare critical signals, versus staying fast. A monitoring agent needs the first.

source: Assessing the three attentional networks and vigilance in the adolescence stages (2021, ANTI-V, 182 adolescents)
finding: ANTI-V in 182 adolescents aged 10 to 19: all networks keep developing, and low vigilance harms alerting and orienting.
numbers: N=182: 58 early (10-14), 87 middle (15-17), 37 late (18-19). Performance improved from early to middle adolescence and began to stabilise late. After 15 a more conservative response strategy and more self-error monitoring. Indirect vigilance indices only moderately correlated with direct measures.
quote: a low level of vigilance seems to harm alerting and orienting abilities
limits: Cross-sectional, unequal groups, one task.
agent_relevance: Alerting and orienting scores partly reflect vigilance, a confound for any network score.

source: Fan, McCandliss, Sommer, Raz, Posner (2002) Testing the efficiency and independence of attentional networks (J Cogn Neurosci 14:340-347)
finding: Founding paper. A cueing task and an arrow flanker task combined, so alerting, orienting and conflict are scored in one test. Authors reported no correlations between network scores but a significant cue by flanker interaction.
numbers: Not opened. As relayed by McConnell and Shore (2011), Habekost et al. (2014) and a search summary: executive score reliable, retest in about 40 adults.
limits: Secondhand only. Check the full PDF before quoting numbers.
agent_relevance: Origin of the three-network scoring used by all later studies.

source: Meta-analysis of attention deficit in primary-school-age children with ADHD measured with the ANT (Front Neurosci 2023)
finding: Seven studies, N=3,826. Children with ADHD differ from controls on alerting but not on executive or orienting scores, though RT and RT variability are larger.
numbers: Hedges g: RT 0.433 (CI 0.135-0.731); RT variability 0.334 (CI 0.012-0.657); alerting 0.235 (CI 0.021-0.449). At-risk children: alerting 0.176 (CI 0.003-0.349). PROSPERO CRD42021249768.
quote: Children with ADHD and at risk of ADHD had different ANT results from children without ADHD only for the alerting network
limits: Abstract only. Few studies; CIs near zero. The expected executive deficit was not found.
agent_relevance: A textbook network story that failed on pooled ANT data.

source: Meta-analysis comparing bilingual and monolingual performance on the attention network test (2020)
finding: Exists (title only). Findings not read.
numbers: None collected.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote effects.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later pass on moderators such as bilingualism.

source: Patel, Wang, Fan (2025) Deficient executive control in transformer attention
finding: GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet saw Stroop word lists as images. Both showed a conflict effect that grew with list length. Incongruent accuracy fell toward or below chance while congruent and word reading stayed high.
numbers: 30 trials per length (1, 5, 10, 20, 40 words) per model; accuracy only, manual scoring. Incongruent colour naming: GPT-4o 91% at 5 words, 57% at 10, 22% at 20, 15% at 40; Claude 76% at 20, 24% at 40. Congruent: 99% at 20, then 89% (GPT-4o) and 92% (Claude) at 40. Mixed lists: GPT-4o 100% at 1, 99% at 5, 72% at 10, 52% at 20, 15% at 40. Humans cited at about 95% and 97% on long lists.
quote: performance degraded toward chance levels on the incongruent trials despite maintaining excellent performance on congruent trials
limits: Two models, image input, hand-built matching of outputs to lists, no reasoning mode. Preprint of March 2025; a PNAS Nexus version was reported by a web search but not opened.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that conflict resolution fails as inputs lengthen. Argues for a separate check step on long inputs. See evidence_c.jsonl for larger VLM Stroop and flanker studies.

source: Patel, Wang, Fan (2025) Deficient executive control in transformer attention
finding: The paper maps ANT theory onto transformers. Self-attention is said to match orienting, extended to semantic dimensions, with no explicit alerting or executive control component.
numbers: Only the executive part was tested. Conditions: congruent, incongruent, mixed, neutral office words, nonword XXX.
limits: Alerting and orienting were not tested. No LLM study found that runs the full ANT with three separate scores. The mapping is an argument, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Gap: an LLM cueing (orienting) and warning-signal (alerting) test has not been run.

source: Kucina et al. (2023) Calibration of cognitive tests to address the reliability paradox for decision-conflict tasks
finding: The authors also combined tasks (Stroop with Simon called Stroopon, Flanker with Simon called Flankon) to get a larger conflict effect, expecting an additive effect in Stroopon and a sub-additive one in Flankon. They also analysed how reliability grows as trials accumulate (48 to 432 trials) on archival Hedge et al. data.
numbers: Trials analysed in steps of 4 blocks of 12 trials: 48, 96, up to 432 trials (36 blocks).
limits: Reliability is the split-half style estimate; longer-interval retest will be lower. MTurk sample.
agent_relevance: Combining conflict sources and counting trials per probe is the practical route to a stable score.
